title: Not to abolish (Matthew 5:17–20)
hook: he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not to destroy them

segments.voice: Yesterday, salt and light, and your line was you are the light. Did you put one good thing on the stand? Day two hundred forty-two.

Some people picture Jesus as the one who came to throw out the old rulebook. Out with all those laws, in with love. It's a popular idea. And it's the very thing Jesus heads off in the next lines of the sermon. Remember who he's talking to: Jews on a hillside in Galilee, who had grown up with the Torah read aloud in the synagogue every Sabbath. They'd been wondering, maybe: is this new teacher against it? So before he says anything else, he answers.
screen: `THROW OUT THE OLD RULEBOOK?` → `A JEWISH CROWD IN GALILEE.` → `BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, HE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." The law here is the Torah, the first five books of the Bible, from Genesis to Deuteronomy. Torah is usually translated law, but the Hebrew word means more like teaching, or instruction: the way God shows people how to live. For Jews, it's the heart of scripture, and it still is. Then Jesus says: till heaven and earth pass, "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled." A jot is the yod, the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet, hardly bigger than an apostrophe. A tittle is a tiny stroke on a letter, the little hook that tells one Hebrew letter from another. Not even that much, he says, will be lost. So what does fulfill mean? Christians have understood it in several ways. Many say Jesus fulfills the law by living it completely, and by bringing out its deepest intent, which the rest of the chapter goes on to do. Many also say that parts of it, like the temple sacrifices, find their fulfillment in him. Churches differ on exactly how the law applies to Christians today, and Jews, for their part, continue to live by the Torah as their covenant with God. Then he says: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. In his day the Pharisees were known for taking the law seriously, down to the details. He isn't lowering the bar. He's saying: go deeper, all the way to the heart.
screen: `TORAH: TEACHING, INSTRUCTION.` · `NOT ONE JOT OR TITTLE.` · `FULFILL: SEVERAL READINGS.` · `DEEPER, TO THE HEART.` · then, large: `NOT TO DESTROY, BUT TO FULFIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your Jewish neighbors' scriptures. Settle, and breathe. The words Jesus is talking about are, first of all, the Torah, still read, sung and studied in synagogues every week. Think of a Jewish neighbor, friend or coworker, or of Jewish families you've never met, gathering around those same scrolls. Hold them in mind with respect and gratitude. If you pray, you can give thanks for the Torah and for the people who have carried it for three thousand years. The bell holds the time.
Torah. The first five books of the Bible; in Hebrew, not just law, but teaching: the way to live. Jesus says he came not to destroy it.
Your line: fulfill, not destroy. Today, when you're tempted to throw out something old, ask first what it was for, and whether you could carry it further. Day two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Christians read the Old Testament in worship alongside the Gospels, and many churches read a passage from the law or the prophets at every Sunday service.

notes: Torah from the root yarah (to throw, aim, teach) is often cited; the script says only 'means more like teaching, or instruction'. Confirm.
'Tittle' (Greek keraia) as a small hook or serif distinguishing Hebrew letters: standard; confirm.
The Pharisees described respectfully as known for careful observance; the script avoids 'hypocrite' stereotypes. Keeper (and ideally a Jewish reader) should confirm tone.
Christian views on how the law applies (moral vs. ceremonial; fulfillment in Christ) described as varied without ranking.
'Three thousand years' for the Torah's tradition is approximate; confirm or soften.
